newsitem.title: FRANCE: France fights new round in privatisation programme.
newsitem.headline: France fights new round in privatisation programme.

text.p: The French government tried to revive a badly shaken privatisation programme on Wednesday when it relaunched the sale of defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF, one of two sell-offs botched last year.
The government said it planned to sell the 58 percent it owns in Thomson-CSF by private placement and participation would be open to French and other European players.

The news came the same day as confirmation that the first stage of a partial sale of France Telecom would take place in May, when 20 percent of the world's fourth largest telecoms operator is due to be offered on the market.
But even if it pulls off the Thomson-CSF sale and the France Telecom sale is the success expected, the government still has a series of tough tasks on its hands.

After abandoning a deal in December to sell off the whole of the Thomson SA - which includes Thomson-CSF and the Thomson Multimedia consumer electronics company -- it still has to decide what to do with the heavily loss-making manufacturer of video and television sets.
At the time, Prime Minister Alain Juppe said that Thomson Multimedia was such a big loss-maker that selling it for one symbolic franc (17 cents) had appeared to be the only option.

Similarly, the finance ministry is looking for ways to privatise regional banking group Credit Industriel et Commercial after halting a sale tender in October which attracted just one eligible offer, from French bank BNP.

Even if the CIC group is profitable, the government's main problem with securing a good price relative to CIC's book value of nearly 15 billion francs was the conditions it imposed on any buyers -- that the group should be held together and its commerical ties with its parent Groupe des Assurances Nationales (GAN) be preserved.

Then comes the formidable task of selling GAN itself, and disposing of beleaguered state-owned bank Credit Lyonnais, which has required successive government bail-outs after a reckless 1980s expansion spree.
Most of these companies need cash injections to make them ready for privatisation.

The centre-right government has committed itself to funding all such cash injections with money raised from privatisations as it tries keep its budget in balance and its public deificit to three percent of grosss domestic product (GDP) this year to qualify for European monetary union.

French newspapers have recently pushed estimates of Credit Lyonnais' needs as high as 30 billion francs and a figure of up to 20 billion for GAN was reported by the daily newspaper Le Monde this month.

The scale of these sums gives an idea of the minimum amount the government needs to raise from privatisations, although neither GAN nor Credit Lyonnais are likely to be knocked into shape to allow their own privatisation in the immediate future.
A France Telecom spokesman said on Wednesday its upcoming privatisation would raise "at least 25 billion francs".

The other complication for the government in sorting out both GAN and Credit Lyonnais is that it has to get clearance, yet again, from the European Commission in Brussels, which has the power to veto state payouts to firms in the European Union.

The finance ministry plans to submit its plans for Credit Lyonnais to the Commission by the end of this week and even before the latest plan had promised Brussels the bank would be privatised early in the next century. ($ = 5.718 French Francs)
